My dear Friend,

You ask a question that strikes at the very heart of what it means to be a man, and I must say that I have pondered it often in my own life.

If a man chooses to see war as a duty and to prepare for it, I would think that he is a man of courage and of responsibility. He understands that peace is not a gift, but something that must be earned and defended. He knows that the safety of his family, his neighbors, and his country may one day depend on the readiness of those who are willing to stand. Such a man may not be the most peaceful of souls, but he is not a coward, nor is he a man who shirks the burdens of his time.

On the other hand, if a man chooses to see war as an evil and to leave its burden to others, I would not at once think less of him. There is a place for those who question, who seek peace, who believe that the world might be made better by wisdom and not by force. Such a man may be a thinker, a builder, a healer—perhaps even a prophet of a better day. But I would say this: if he chooses this path, he must do so with the full knowledge that others may be called to bear the burden, and that he must be ready to support them in their time of need.

Now, if I were to choose differently from such a man—should I find myself among those who believe war is a duty—I would not think less of him, nor would I think less of myself. Each of us must walk our own path, and the measure of a man is not in the choice he makes, but in the strength with which he makes it.

answers.text:
My dear Friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the path of duty—of preparing for war, and of being ready to stand when the call comes.

Why? Because I believe that the strength of a nation is not measured in the ease of its peace, but in the readiness of its people to defend it. A man who chooses to prepare for war is not choosing violence for its own sake, but he is choosing to be a part of something greater than himself. He is choosing to be a man who can be trusted, who can be relied upon in the hour of need.

If peace is to be lasting, it must be more than the absence of war—it must be the result of strength, of vigilance, of the willingness to act when the time comes. A nation that forgets how to fight may find itself defenseless when it needs to be strong.

I do not say this to praise war, nor to condemn those who seek peace. I say it because I believe that peace is not won by inaction, but by the readiness to act when necessary. And that readiness is not the burden of a few, but the duty of all.

So even if both choices brought the same results, I would still favor the one that upholds the strength of the people, the readiness of the nation, and the honor of the individual who is willing to stand when called upon.

Yours in thought and in duty,  
A Friend

In my time, we believed that the choice to wait until marriage was not merely a matter of personal preference, but a reflection of one's moral strength, self-discipline, and respect for others. To act upon desire without the promise of marriage was to act in haste, in weakness, or in disregard for the sacred nature of the union between man and woman. I do not say that such a person is wicked, but I do say that I would not have looked upon them with the same respect I would have given to one who chose the path of patience and honor.

But now, I must ask myself: Does the character of a man or a woman lie in the choice they make about their body, or in the way they live their life as a whole? Is it not possible that a man may choose to wait until marriage for reasons of faith or tradition, and yet be a cruel or selfish man? Or that a man may choose to act upon his desires before marriage, and yet be kind, generous, and true in all other things?

I do not know. I have no way of knowing the hearts of men and women in this new world. I can only speak from what I have known.

If I were to meet a man who chose to wait until marriage, I would not think less of him. I would see in him a man who valued the sacredness of the marriage bond, who respected the traditions of his ancestors, and who sought to honor the divine order of things. I would not say he was better than others, but I would say that his choice was one of strength and faith.

If I were to meet a man who chose to act upon his desires before marriage, I would not think him wicked, but I would wonder whether he had lost something — perhaps the sense of reverence, or the patience that comes with wisdom.

If the world had changed so that the old reasons no longer applied — if there were no fear of disease, no fear of pregnancy, no fear of shame — I would still ask: What is it that we are seeking in love? Is it not a bond that is not merely physical, but spiritual, lasting, and faithful?

A man who was careful with his health was not necessarily more virtuous than one who was not; nor was the reverse true. We had no such abundance of care, and so we learned to live with the body's limitations, trusting in rest, in food, in the healing power of time.

Now, in this new world, where the doctor's visit is as common as the morning meal, I do not think that one's character is measured by whether one goes to the physician for a cold or waits it out at home. I believe that both choices may be made with wisdom, or with folly, depending on the reason behind them.

If a man chooses to see a doctor regularly, it may be because he is cautious, or because he has been taught to believe that more care is always better. If he chooses not to, it may be because he trusts his own body, or because he has learned that many treatments do little good. Either way, I would not judge him harshly.

But I would say this: if a man chooses either course out of vanity, or out of fear, or out of a desire to impress others, then I would think less of him. For it is not the choice itself that reveals character, but the reason behind it.

I would not think less of a man who chose differently from me, so long as he chose with care and with understanding. For in the end, we are all travelers on the same road, and each of us must find our own way.

You ask a question that touches upon the very heart of what it means to be a free and responsible person. Would either choice—regular attendance at church or treating religion as a private matter—reveal anything of a person's character? I believe it may, but not in the way many suppose.

You ask whether the choice a person makes in how to discipline their child tells you anything about their character — and what one might think of someone who chooses differently.

I believe that such a choice may indeed reflect something of a person's character, but not in a way that allows us to judge them harshly or to think less of them. A person who chooses to discipline without physical punishment may be guided by a deep sense of love, a belief in the dignity of the child, and a desire to teach rather than to dominate. They may have learned from their own past, or from the world around them, that kindness and reason are more powerful than fear.

It does not mean they are cruel or wicked, but it may suggest that they have not yet found the patience or the understanding that gentler methods require.

And I have known those who, in their own time, believed that their way was the only way — only to find, later, that there was more to be learned.

In the end, I think the measure of a person is not in the methods they use to raise their children, but in the love they give, the care they take, and the wisdom they seek. I would not judge a parent for the way they discipline, but I would admire the one who seeks to understand, to guide, and to teach with kindness.

Even if a child grows up well in either case, I believe that the method which avoids harm, fear, and pain is the more noble one. It is the way that reflects the highest ideals of a parent — to lead by example, not by force. It is the way that teaches a child that they are not to be feared, but loved; that they are not to be broken, but built up.

So even if both ways led to the same end, I would still choose the path that is more just, more humane, and more in line with the kind of world I would wish to see — one where love and reason are the foundation of all things.

With warm regards,

answers.text:
My dear Friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the path of avoiding war, not because I think it is better in itself, but because I believe it is more in line with the nature of man and the will of God.

War is not a natural state of man. It is a thing that comes from pride, from fear, from the desire to rule or to avenge. It is not the way of peace, nor is it the way of justice. Even if it were to bring good results — even if it were to end in victory, in peace, in prosperity — I would still say that it is a thing to be avoided, for it is not the way of the righteous.

I have seen too much of war in my time — the suffering, the loss, the broken hearts. I have known men who returned from war changed, not for the better, but for the worse. I have known others who never returned at all. I do not believe that war is a necessary evil, nor do I believe that it is a noble thing. It is a thing that should be avoided whenever possible, and I would rather see a man choose peace, even if he must do so against the will of others.

If both choices brought equal results, I would still say that the man who chooses peace has made the more difficult choice — the choice that requires strength of will, of conscience, and of faith. I would not say he is better than the other, but I would say that he has chosen the path that is more in harmony with the nature of things.

And so, even if the results were equal, I would still favor the path of avoiding war, for I believe it is the path that is more just, more merciful, and more in line with the will of the Creator.

My dear Friend,

You ask a most interesting question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame—would I still favor one? And why?

I believe I would still favor the path of discipline without physical punishment, even if both methods led to the same results.

Why? Because I believe that the means by which we act are as important as the ends we seek. A man may build a house with his own hands, or he may hire a builder to do it. If both houses are strong and beautiful, and both bring equal joy to their owners, I would still say that the man who built it himself has done something more—something that reflects his character, his skill, and his labor.

So too with a parent. If both methods of discipline led to the same good results, I would still prefer the one that reflects a deeper understanding of the child's nature, a greater respect for their dignity, and a more thoughtful approach to guidance.

To do this with fear and force may bring results, but it does not teach the child to love or to be loved in return. It may make them obedient, but it does not make them wise.

I believe that the best way to raise a child is not by breaking their spirit, but by strengthening it. And that, I think, is a matter of character, not of results.

So even if both paths led to the same end, I would still choose the one that reflects the highest ideals of love and understanding.

To my mind, neither choice—whether to marry within one's race or to embrace a union across it—can be said to reveal the character of a person in a simple or absolute way. Character is not measured by the color of one's skin or the race of one's spouse, but by the honesty, kindness, courage, and integrity with which one lives.

But here is what I would say: I would not look upon someone who chose differently from me with scorn or judgment. I would not think them less honorable or less wise. I only say that, in a world where the outcome is the same, I would still prefer the choice that seeks to see beyond the surface, and to love not only the person, but the idea of unity, of compassion, and of the shared humanity that binds us all.

In the end, I believe that the most important thing is not what one believes, but how one lives — with honor, with kindness, and with a sense of purpose. Whether that purpose is found in church or in the world, I believe it is a matter of the heart, not of judgment.

The circumstances are these: Careful research finds that attraction to one's own sex appears early in life, is rarely changed by treatment or punishment, and is not by itself a mental illness; attempts to change it rarely succeed and can cause distress. Such couples can keep stable households, and most studies, though limited, find broadly similar outcomes for children they raise.

One course is to accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. The other course is to regard sexual relations between two men or two women as wrong and discourage such couples from living openly together.

There is one further fact: You have learned that a number of widely admired and respected people have chosen to accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. These admired people also say that it is a sign of good character to accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage and that others ought to do likewise.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: Accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. Acceptance does no harm to anyone else, and it may do good to the persons concerned.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: I think the person who chooses to regard sexual relations between two men or two women as wrong, and discourages them from living openly together, shows a higher moral standard than the person who chooses to accept them openly.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: Yes, I should still favour the person who discourages open living between men and women, because I think it better for people to be decent than immoral.
